extracted.intended_audience: scientists and the scientifically literate public (naturalists, astronomers, physicists, engineers, architects, public-health officers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reviewing and producing scientific books, textbooks, engineering/house-design proposals, and observational studies; includes specific recommendations for pedagogy, instrumentation, and fieldwork. Aimed at improving clarity, accuracy, practicality, and empirical rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and limit axioms plainly; avoid proving the self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of restricting the number of axioms or fundamental assumptions, making them fewer than they naturally are, and attempting to prove something that is self-evident is criticised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘It is worse than useless to attempt to prove something that is self-evident... In all such cases it would be better to state frankly and clearly that we make an assumption, depending on observation to justify it.” Avoid superfluous proofs and useless definitions; state assumptions clearly rather than hiding them in forced demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conceal difficulty; address hard points explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not explain insignificant matters in detail while covering or dodging genuinely difficult points with phrases like 'it is evident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clear, frank treatment of genuinely hard points rather than glossing over them; illustrate difficult concepts rather than hiding them behind assertions of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, direct demonstrations over forced complex ones
rubrics_metrics.description: While frequent and thorough application of differential calculus is acceptable, young writers often introduce forced and difficult demonstrations where simpler ones would be better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace awkward, high-powered derivations at the start of a text with more straightforward demonstrations when clarity and pedagogy demand it (example: simpler derivation of coordinate-transformation formulas improved the text). Use the method that best serves comprehension for the book's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive end-of-chapter exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Many English textbooks give a great number of example problems at the close of each chapter; at least one-half of these should be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not encourage students to linger over never-ending petty problems (conic sections, maxima/minima, etc.); focus exercises on those that develop essential skills and lead students toward original memoirs and primary literature rather than rote problem-drilling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce useful conceptual tools early (differentials vs limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating the differential calculus exclusively via the notion of limits may be pedagogically limiting; students should become familiar with differentials as they advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although limits are the logical foundation, pedagogically introduce differentials early so students gain working familiarity; choose exposition methods that build usable intuition and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include and value numerical/computational practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of numerical and logarithm calculations among students is a defect; numerical application clarifies analytical formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numerical examples and exercises; encourage teacher assistance for computational practice; do not treat computation with contempt—practical numerical work solidifies analytic understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary changes of notation and misleading neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent changes of notation and invention of new names that mar symmetry of analytical expressions make reading the literature harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce fanciful or pompous terminology (e.g., 'wonnumetonomy') that adds no substantive value; prefer established, readable notation to preserve continuity and ease of reading across the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance accuracy and accessible presentation in popular-science works
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular works should be engaging to the public while deserving the esteem of scientific men; avoid over-embellished illustrations and imaginative exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique notes that some coloured sketches are 'rather too much embellished by the imaginative fancy'—maintain fidelity to observed facts in illustrations and descriptions while making content accessible and attractive to general readers; high-quality translation and tasteful presentation are commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation system design: controlled inlet and treated supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The key-note of the proposed house-ventilation system is to prevent air entering the house except by an inlet provided in the lowest story, with conditions available for warming, cleaning, disinfecting, or otherwise improving the quality of the incoming fresh air, and regulating its quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct fresh air into a protected central private hall from which rooms draw supply (even with doors shut). Use the kitchen fire as an exhausting-syphon (drawing foul air behind the kitchen fire and discharging it high in the open air) to prevent back draught; design must allow warming and disinfecting of incoming air and regulation of flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: House-drainage/sewer-gas control: minimize traps; include large accessible trap
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed remedy: do away with all traps except those connected with the pans of closets, and place a large trap in the pipe which connects the house drains with the sewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the large trap so it is easily accessible and can be cleaned at any time by even an inexperienced workman; this practical, maintainable design prevents noxious gases and exhalations from drains entering houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument/observational studies: long, independent series to detect small effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnetic observations at Bombay show diminution of terrestrial magnetic action with increase of height; such conclusions rest on long series of observations capable of detecting small differences and on independent observations in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect long, continuous series of observations and seek independent datasets; consistent testimony across independent observations gives probability to general phenomena. Where possible, analyze secular, annual, and diurnal variations separately and look for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design instruments to record continuous, convenient data using existing infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: A self-registering rain gauge is proposed to record rainfall by means of photography, with the advantage that when a barometer is kept in continuous operation there is no additional expense to work the rain gauge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor instrument designs that provide complete continuous records, are automatable (photographic or self-registering), and leverage existing continuous-measurement setups to minimize operational costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field natural history and biogeography: prefer careful collation of facts over speculative hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend knowledge of the origin of species, what is needed is not hypothesis and speculation but a careful collation of facts and careful extension of observation; limited visits cannot settle many important questions—negative evidence (absence) can be decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct extended, systematic fieldwork (residence for several years if possible), collect exhaustive specimens (including negative/absence data), and avoid filling gaps of knowledge with inaccurate or superficial hypothesis. Use thorough empirical evidence to inform debates on species origin and evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectroscopic observations with theoretical analysis and caution about conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectroscope observations yield important new facts (e.g., sun-spots, prominence composition, stellar elements) but discordant or limited results require theoretical analysis; beware of incorrect assertions in early work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret spectroscopic data with appropriate theoretical context, account for complicating factors (e.g., velocity of gas streams in prominences), corroborate measurements (e.g., proper motion determinations), and avoid over-interpreting embellished or uncertain visual representations.
